pharm: Competitive antagonist at pituitary GnRH receptors; suppresses LH (and to a lesser extent FSH) to prevent premature LH surges
quick: 0.25 mg SC daily, or 3 mg SC single dose
Contraindicated; do not use while nursing
summary: Cetrorelix is a synthetic decapeptide GnRH antagonist used during controlled ovarian stimulation (COS) to prevent premature LH surges and thus premature ovulation, preserving oocyte quality for IVF/ICSI. Unlike GnRH agonists it produces immediate, dose-dependent suppression of LH without an initial flare. It is given subcutaneously either as a single 3 mg dose (protection of at least 4 days) or as 0.25 mg once daily until the day of hCG trigger. LH suppression is reversible after discontinuation, and FSH levels are largely unaffected at therapeutic doses. It should be prescribed by clinicians experienced in fertility treatment, and pregnancy must be excluded before starting.
indications: Inhibition of premature LH surges in women undergoing controlled ovarian stimulation (assisted reproductive technology / IVF-ICSI)

dosage.c: Premature LH surge prevention - multiple-dose regimen
dosage.t: Start stimulation day 5 (AM or PM) or day 6 (AM); continue daily until and including the day of hCG
dosage.n: Given during early- to mid-follicular phase alongside gonadotropins (FSH/hMG started cycle day 2-3)

dosage.c: Premature LH surge prevention - single-dose regimen
dosage.t: On the COS day when adequate estradiol (about 400 pg/mL) is reached, usually day 7 (range day 5-12)
dosage.n: Provides at least 4 days protection; if hCG is not given within 4 days, add 0.25 mg SC daily starting 96 h after the 3 mg dose until and including the day of hCG

admin: For subcutaneous injection only, after reconstitution with the supplied Sterile Water for Injection
Reconstitute by injecting the solvent into the vial and gently swirling until clear; avoid forming bubbles; discard any unused portion
Draw up with the 20-gauge (yellow) needle, then switch to the 27-gauge (grey) needle and expel air before injecting
Inject into the lower abdomen at least one inch (about 2.5 cm) away from the navel; rotate sites daily to limit local irritation
Clean the site with alcohol and let it dry; gently pinch up the skin before injecting
May be self-administered after appropriate training by the clinician
Use each syringe and needle only once and dispose of in a sharps/medical-waste container
moa: Cetrorelix is an analog of native gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) with amino-acid substitutions at positions 1, 2, 3, 6 and 10. It competes with endogenous GnRH for binding to membrane receptors on anterior-pituitary gonadotroph cells, dose-dependently suppressing the release of luteinizing hormone (LH) and, to a lesser extent, follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). By blocking the midcycle estradiol-driven LH surge, it prevents premature ovulation and luteinization during ovarian stimulation. As a pure antagonist it causes no initial gonadotropin flare, and its effect is rapid in onset (about 1 hour with the 3 mg dose, 2 hours with 0.25 mg) and fully reversible after discontinuation.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to cetrorelix acetate, extrinsic peptide hormones, or mannitol
Known hypersensitivity to GnRH or any other GnRH analog
relative: Active allergic conditions or known allergic predisposition (avoid in severe allergic conditions)
Should be prescribed only by physicians experienced in fertility treatment
monitor: Hypersensitivity/anaphylactoid reactions (can occur with first dose)
Liver enzymes (ALT, AST, GGT, alkaline phosphatase)

preg: Contraindicated in pregnancy; pregnancy must be excluded before starting therapy. In animal studies, doses near or above the human therapeutic exposure caused increased resorptions and complete post-implantation loss, consistent with the drug's antigonadotropic effect, which could cause fetal loss in humans. No increase in fetal malformations was seen in pregnancies that were maintained.
lact: Contraindicated during lactation. It is unknown whether cetrorelix is excreted in human milk, and effects on the breastfed infant have not been determined; do not use in nursing mothers.
renal: Contraindicated in severe renal impairment. Pharmacokinetics have not been studied in patients with impaired renal function. Elimination is partly renal (about 2-4% of a dose excreted unchanged in urine), so accumulation is a concern in renal failure.
hepatic: Pharmacokinetics have not been studied in hepatic impairment, so no specific dosing guidance exists; use with caution. Asymptomatic transaminase/GGT/alkaline phosphatase elevations up to 3 times the upper limit of normal were seen in 1-2% of treated patients during ovarian stimulation, of uncertain clinical significance.

interactions.food: Not applicable; given by subcutaneous injection.
interactions.alcohol: No specific alcohol interaction described in the labeling.
interactions.diagnostics: No formal drug-drug interaction studies have been performed. During gonadotropin stimulation, cetrorelix has no notable effect on hormone levels other than suppressing the LH surge.

common: Injection-site reactions (redness, erythema, bruising, itching, swelling, pruritus) - usually mild and transient
serious: Hypersensitivity / anaphylactoid reactions, including with the first dose
rare: Severe anaphylactic reaction (cough, rash, hypotension) reported with prolonged high-dose use in a non-fertility setting
emergency: Anaphylaxis / severe hypersensitivity with hypotension and respiratory symptoms
Severe OHSS (marked abdominal distension, dyspnea, oliguria, thromboembolism)

monitoring: Transvaginal ultrasound for follicle number and size to time the hCG trigger
Serum estradiol and LH during stimulation
Signs and symptoms of OHSS; withhold hCG if ovaries show excessive response
Watch for hypersensitivity/anaphylactoid reactions, including after the first dose
Liver enzymes (ALT, AST, GGT, alkaline phosphatase) given reported elevations
Confirm pregnancy is excluded before initiating treatment
counsel: This medicine prevents your ovaries from releasing eggs too early during fertility treatment
It is given as a small injection just under the skin of the lower belly, at least an inch away from the navel; rotate the spot each day
If self-injecting, follow the reconstitution and injection steps you were taught and use each needle only once
With the daily 0.25 mg regimen, inject at about the same time each day until your clinic tells you to stop (day of the trigger shot)
Tell your clinic right away about rash, itching, swelling, difficulty breathing, or feeling faint after an injection
Report severe bloating, abdominal pain, rapid weight gain, nausea, or shortness of breath (possible OHSS)
Do not use if you are or might be pregnant, or while breastfeeding
pk: LH suppression about 1 h (3 mg dose); about 2 h (0.25 mg dose)
Tmax about 1-2 h after SC injection
About 62.8 h (3 mg single dose); about 5 h (0.25 mg single), about 20.6 h (0.25 mg multiple)
At least 4 days after a single 3 mg dose; 0.25 mg every 24 h maintains the effect
Refrigerate 2-8 C (36-46 F); protect from light in the outer carton
pearls: Pure GnRH antagonist: immediate LH suppression with no agonist 'flare,' allowing a shorter, more flexible stimulation protocol than agonist down-regulation
Two regimens: a single 3 mg dose (protects at least 4 days) or 0.25 mg daily until the hCG trigger
With the 3 mg regimen, if hCG is delayed beyond 4 days, bridge with 0.25 mg daily starting 96 h after the 3 mg dose
Effect on FSH is minimal at therapeutic doses, so ongoing follicular growth from gonadotropins is preserved
Withhold hCG if ovarian response is excessive to reduce OHSS risk
Subcutaneous bioavailability is high (about 85%); plasma protein binding about 86%
missed: For the 0.25 mg daily regimen, give the missed dose as soon as remembered and continue the daily schedule; do not double up. Because uninterrupted dosing maintains LH suppression, contact the fertility clinic for guidance if a dose is missed, as timing relative to the hCG trigger is critical.
overdose: No cases of overdose with the 0.25 mg or 3 mg doses have been reported in humans. Single doses up to 120 mg have been well tolerated in patients treated for other indications without signs of overdosage. Management is supportive.
